newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel wants deep cuts for 1998 German budget - TV.
newsitem.headline: Waigel wants deep cuts for 1998 German budget - TV.

text.p: Finance Minister Theo Waigel told German television on Sunday he wants to radically cut spending and push through the privatisation of further government assets to help Bonn balance its books in 1998.
Waigel also said he was sure savings at both federal and state level this year would mean Germany would meet the entry criteria needed to qualify for Europe's single currency.
"I will present my budget plan (for 1998) on July 10, Waigel told NTV news television, according to a release ahead of the airing of an interview with him on Sunday evening.

Waigel said Bonn must make "unbelievable savings" and said Chancellor Helmut Kohl's ruling coalition would explore which subsidies could be cut, adding everything would have to be considered and there could be no "taboos".

Waigel defended plans to sell more of Bonn's stake in telecommunications giant Deutsche Telekom to an intermediary organisation, the Kreditanstalt fuer Wiederaufbau, to avoid harming the prospects of Telekom shares.

Although Waigel is in the midst of preparing his 1998 budget, soaring unemployment and lower-than-expected tax receipts have meant he may not be able to balance the books in 1997 -- the year which will determine which countries take part in the first wave of European economic and monetary union.
Waigel said if planned savings were not enough to stop a gaping hole in this year's budget, Bonn would have to pass a supplementary budget.
Waigel on Saturday ruled out increasing government new debt in 1998, saying total borrowing in the year must remain under 58 to 59 billion marks ($34-35 billion).
The German constitution requires that new government borrowing does not exceed total public investment, which Waigel expects to be around 59 billion marks in 1998, a figure similar to this year's.
